strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—monitoring deployed models when labels are scarce—and proposes a clean semi-supervised extension of supervised risk monitoring (SRM) via prediction-powered inference (PPI), generalizing Podkopaev & Ramdas (2022) to streams with both labeled and unlabeled batches.

The statistical guarantees are rigorous and well-structured: Lemma 3.1 establishes unbiasedness of the prediction-powered running-risk estimator for any predictable sequence of reliance parameters ηt, and Theorem 3.2 inherits assumption-free anytime-valid type-I error control from the SRM framework. The predictability requirement is handled carefully via a sliding-window plug-in estimator (27).

The adaptive selection of ηt via variance minimization (Lemma 3.3 / PPI++-style optimal η) is a sensible and empirically validated addition, with the ablation in Table 1 and Figures 12–13 showing that adaptivity prevents degradation with weak predictors.

Experiments span three domains (image classification on CIFAR10-C, LLM QA with LLM-as-a-judge imputation, and a wireless channel-equalization task), including a self-synthetic setting where the deployed model itself imputes labels, and the empirical false-alarm curve in Figure 5 empirically validates the type-I error guarantee.

The appendix contains a thoughtful approximate detection-delay analysis (Proposition A.1) that clarifies the trade-off between variance reduction and the range-normalization penalty (1+2η)², plus an extension to intermittent label streams that interpolates between supervised and unsupervised monitoring.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely a composition of existing techniques—PPI/PPI++ variance-optimal imputation, CM-EB anytime-valid confidence sequences (Howard et al., 2021), and the SRM decision framework of Podkopaev & Ramdas (2022)—so the methodological novelty is incremental. The relationship to concurrent prediction-powered e-value approaches for sequential testing (Csillag et al., 2025) is discussed but the comparison is only conceptual.

Empirical gains over SRM are often modest: e.g., alarm times of ~760 vs ~800 (Figure 2a), ~760 vs ~790 (Figure 2b), and ~500 vs ~530 (Figure 3), with overlapping inter-run variability in the box plots. No statistical significance analysis of the detection-delay differences is provided.

The baseline set is thin: comparisons are against SRM, URM (Schirmer et al., 2025), and an idealized oracle, but the unsupervised method of Amoukou et al. (2024) and betting/e-value based sequential change detectors (Shekhar & Ramdas, 2023) are not empirically compared despite being discussed as related alternatives.

The setting requires at least one labeled sample at every time step (nt strictly positive), which is a practical limitation for the motivating 'labels are costly' narrative; this is acknowledged implicitly (Section 3.1) but its implications and the labeling-cost trade-off are not analyzed in the main text, and there is no explicit limitations section.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several experimental details (number of trials, exact shift constructions, how LLM prompt shifts are sampled per trial) are underspecified relative to the level of detail needed to replicate Figures 2–5.
